passage: Saturday: Rohan's kite kept spinning in circles. He added a longer tail and flew it once. It still wobbled, but it spun less. Sunday: he changed only the place where the string was tied, a finger-width lower, and flew it again. It leaned and dipped. 'Wrong way,' he said, and put it back. Monday: he left the string where it was and made the tail longer still, and now the kite stood steady over the field. His sister Sudha asked why he never changed both at once. 'Then I wouldn't know which one helped,' said Rohan. He wrote 'long tail = steady' on the reel.

passage:
Leela, come, sit. Your Tenzin Popo will tell you about kites. When I was a boy in Kalimpong, maybe ten, I had a red kite that would not fly straight. It spun and dived every time.
My friends kept changing everything at once: new tail, new string, new paper. Their kites never got better, and they never knew why.
I did it differently. First flight, I only made the tail longer by one hand. Better. Second flight, same tail, I moved the string knot a little lower. Worse. So I moved it back. Third flight, even longer tail. Steady as a hawk.
One change, one flight, and watch. That is how I learned the tail was the secret. Later, when I became an engineer, I did exactly the same with machines.

qa.q: How much longer did Tenzin make the tail on the first flight?
qa.a: Tenzin made the tail longer by one hand.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel when the kite flew steady on the third flight?
qa.a: Tenzin felt proud and satisfied, since he had found out for sure that the longer tail was the secret.

qa.q: At the second flight, what choice did Tenzin make, and why was it a good one?
qa.a: When moving the string made things worse, he moved it back, so he could keep testing with only one thing changed at a time.

qa.q: How might Tenzin's friends have felt watching his kite fly steady?
qa.a: They may have been puzzled or jealous, since they changed everything at once and never knew what worked.

grounding: It shows a boy tuning a kite by changing one thing per flight, so he learns that a longer tail steadies it.

It was the last hour of daylight before Makar Sankranti, and Sumit had only one spool of string left. His kite kept flipping over the rooftops.
Hrithik said, "Change the tail and the string and the paper, quick!"
"No," Sumit said. "Then I won't know what worked."
He added one strip of old sari to the tail and flew it. Less flipping, but still wobbly. He landed it, added another strip, and flew again. Better. Then he tried moving the string knot up. It spun at once. He moved the knot back.
By the time the sky turned orange, the kite hung steady above the water tank. Sumit wrote on his hand: long tail, knot low.

qa.q: What did Sumit write on his hand?
qa.a: He wrote long tail, knot low.

qa.q: Why did Sumit refuse to change everything at once?
qa.a: He was calm and determined, wanting to know for sure which change made the difference, even with little time left.

qa.q: What would change if Sumit had followed Hrithik's advice?
qa.a: The kite might have flown, but Sumit would not know whether the tail, string or paper fixed it, so he could not repeat it next time.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see Sumit's slow way of testing?
qa.a: Hrithik may find it frustratingly slow at first, but then see that the steady kite and the note on Sumit's hand came from it.

grounding: It shows a boy changing one thing on his kite per flight and learning that a longer tail steadies it.
